Oudtshoorn

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Two years after losing their seats on the Oudtshoorn town council, members of the now minority ANC/NPP coalition flatly refuse to vacate their posts - the town hovers on the brink of bankruptcy

Summary:
Oudtshoorn is on a knife edge with politicians on all sides pleading for national governement and senior ANC intervention. We expect motion of no-confidence this coming week in municipal manager Ronnie Lottering. Speaker John Sotffels surprisingly resigned last week.

We investigate allegations that Mayor Gordon April, Ronnie Lottering and publicity consultant Drewan Baird have been manipulating the system, holding on to power for personal gain - running the council like their personal fiefdom.

The council stopped working two years ago after the ANC-coalition refused to hand over power to the DA-COPE coalition. Municipal budgets are not being passed - resulting in the non-payment of services - for instance, in less than a month, the town is due to be disconnected form the electicity grid by ESKOM to whom it owes around R25-million.

The local river, a water source for the region, is being polluted by raw sewage, as service provision grinds to a halt.

Money has been misallocated from the budget of the Cango Caves - an important regional, if not national, tourist attraction and significant income earner.

The council has refused to hold meetings; suspended councillors for no reason; allegedly used public money in litigation as a delaying tactic; have allegedly offered inducements to other councillors in exchange for votes; and have ignored court orders.

Protests flared in March when municipal workers heard the municipality had allegedly stolen their pension and medical aid contributions.

It reached fever pitch this week when fisticuffs broke out in the council chamber after town councillors failed to approve the municipality’s budget for the third time in two months. The public gallery got involved in barricading councillors for two hours after the DA voted against the budget and the ANC abstained.

Both the ANC and the DA-led provincial government put out statements pleading with Cooperative Governance Minister Pravin Gordhan to intervene.

Further information:
The town council became paralysed by infighting after May 2013, when the DA seized control of the ANC-run municipality -- five ANC councillors voted with the DA in a motion of no confidence in the speaker, mayor and deputy mayor.

In September 2013 the Western Cape High Court ruled that the DA’s ‘takeover’ of the Oudtshoorn municipality in this manner was illegitimate. By then, however, by-elections had handed the DA a clear council majority in a coalition with Cope. Subsequent by-elections have also seen the ANC lose. In May this year, the DA won another ward. The DA has a council majority on paper, but the ANC in coalition with some smaller parties steadfastly refuses to relinquish power.

In May, DA Western Cape leader Patricia de Lille wrote to President Jacob Zuma to intervene.

The ANC Western Cape leader Marius Fransman has suggested that the council may need to be dissolved.

Gordhan did visit the municipality in March and proposed a "support and good governance package", which the municipality subsequently failed to adopt. Such a package would include the appointment of an experienced municipal manager, and would also seek to resolve outstanding legal matters affecting municipal operations.

In June, a letter signed by all the DA councillors in the municipality and seven out of the 10 ANC councillors called for the adoption of Gordhan's package and they stated that their concern for the state of the municipality transcended their party affiliations.

Gordhan has said that he would be visiting Outdshoorn again to discuss the implementation of government support.

ANC Western Cape local government spokesperson Richard Dyanti called on councillors to work with Gordhan “to ensure the rescue package put together for the Little Karoo town is put in motion to work optimally for the people”.

Western Cape MEC Bredell, meanwhile, noted “with concern” the “continued instability” in the Oudtshoorn council, and said that he remained in “continuous consultation” with Minister Gordhan.

Press Release:


Oudsthoorn on a Knife-Edge
Oudtshoorn is a jewel on the Garden Route. This gateway to the Klein Karoo is also home to the Cango Caves World Heritage Site. But peel back the peaceful veneer, and what’s revealed, is a town held hostage by apparent vested interests and political expediency. Carte Blanche investigates a meltdown of local governance that threatens to devastate one of the country’s top tourism destinations


Script:


PROMOS
10 seconds
With the Cango Caves coffers bled dry – can it stay open for visitors?
HEIN GERSTNER: it’s very alarming to run a business if you have no control over your cash flow.

15 secs
Democracy under threat in the beautiful Garden Route – who is really running Oudtshoorn?
HARDY: the DA is the biggest party, ANC is second best, but there’s no doubt that the municipality is being controlled and run by the two small parties.

15 secs
Residents of historic Oudtshoorn, home of the Cango Caves, cry out for help with their municipality.
PRAVIN GORDHAN: If we’re not looking after treasures like that in a municipal area…how can we say we’re governing a town in a decent and correct kind of way?

OUDTSHOORN SCRIPT
JOHN: Oudtshoorn is one of the Jewels on the Garden Route, Gateway to the Klein Karoo. But peel back the peaceful veneer, and what’s revealed, is a town held hostage by apparent vested interests and political expedience.
MR X: What happened here is that on the Tuesday night… of this council meeting…is that people were transported to this specific council meeting… with Ronnie Lottering’s Fortuner.
Mr X is a longtime resident of Oudtshoorn. Together with some councillors who wouldn’t go on camera, he said Municipal Manager Ronnie Lottering is the man who broke democracy in this town.
Mr X: What happened here is that THOMAS tried to fight inside the council meeting to approve the budget. THOMAS is an element of the Americans.
JOHN: So these are gangsters were talking about?
MR X: Yes, he is a gangster.
JOHN: You mention that you know what’s happening here because this is a role that you filled in the past.
MR X: I was used repeatedly, phoned to come and transport the people. I collected people from the refuse dump...around 60 or 70 men that I transported. I was given R1000 now and then to give the men, then I used about R150 for fuel and the other R800 I gave the men.
Municipalities all around South Africa face a crisis of capacity and corruption. When he assumed the Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs ministry last year, Pravin Gordhan undertook a thorough assessment of the job ahead.
MINISTER PRAVIN GORDHAN, COOPERATIVE GOVERNANCE & TRADITIONAL AFFAIRS: we undertook an extensive desktop and sometimes physical study of municipalities – all 278 of them – categorised them into those that are doing well, those that are reasonably well but need to repair one or two things and those that are doing poorly – display some levels of dysfunctionality. Oudtshoorn stuck out as a sore thumb…
The semi-arid Oudtshoorn, with its nearly 100-thousand residents rely on tourism and agriculture for survival – mismanaging resources could bring suffering that would be hard to recover from.
Newspaper publisher Schalk le Roux has seen the rift between Oudtshoorn local municipality and its people widen.
SCHALK LE ROUX, DIE HOORN PUBLISHER: At one point I even called it a hoodlum regime. They do exactly as they please. Processes aren’t followed – like with the appointment of people. When goods are purchased they don’t follow tender processes. They are just not accountable.
The governance meltdown threatens one of our greatest national treasures. Archaeologist Hein Gerstner pours his heart and soul into stewarding the Cango Caves.
JOHN: Hein, talk about the paper trail. What are we dealing with here?
HEIN GERSTNER: Each and every one of these documents is an outcry over a number of years to say, what is happening under the municipal auspices, is not conducive to the caves and this is basically a plea to change that…
The Caves have always been managed as a part of Oudtshoorn municipality. After 1994 surplus funds from admission fees and a loan taken out to build the museum complex was saved in an investment account – reserves for future cave maintenance and development.
HEIN GERSTNER: In 2011 you noticed there’s an R17-million, R17,7-million in that particular fund.
JOHN: These totals are substantially down from previous years, but I guess is it any wonder if you for example a figure of R5-million flowing out of the account?
HEIN GERSTNER: At certain points this was reduced to a R139, which is…it’s very alarming to run a business if you have no control over your cash flow.
A year ago Hein first blew the whistle on the dwindling millions, begging anyone who would listen to take the caves and the funds they generate from the municipality’s control.
JOHN: What’s your best guess what this money is used for, why is it going to the municipality in the first place.
HEIN GERSTNER: Well I can’t even speculate. I think it’s only for running the Municipality in general, because the situation is so desperate and dire.
JOHN: So the caves are somewhat of a cash cow, “its money that’s there, let’s use the money”.
President of Oudtshoorn’s tourism authority Niel Els says in the current economic climate, bad publicity threatens the whole region.
NIEL ELS: The economic impact of the Cango caves on a small town like Oudtshoorn is annually round about 400 million and that’s only if you take the average visitor to the Cango Caves will only stay one night on Oudtshoorn. So we are really adamant that the Municipality should sort out their problems, so we can go ahead and market this town as best as possible.
HEIN GERSTNER: I’m in my 23rd year of running the caves and I can’t constantly be fighting this battle just to keep the coffers open and the business open.
JOHN: What are the consequences for you of talking to us?
HEIN GERSTNER: It will be interesting to see but I feel it’s my responsibility as the custodian of that heritage and…you…(chokes up, gets up and walks away)
At the end of his tether – Gerstner faces declining visitor numbers…a drained bank account…and desperate creditors, owed over R4-million for new light installations. The caves budget should be signed off by the local council by no later than the thirtieth of June every year. But for the last two years this and other council business has all but ground to a halt.
JOHN: In-fighting in the Oudsthoorn Municipality has brought service delivery to a standstill. Roads, sewage, electricity, all have been impacted by the rot.
MOTORIST VOXIE: Everything is done cheaply and in the long run the motorist suffers – check the potholes in the road.
PEDESTRIAN VOXIE: It’s been re-done 10 times. It’s money-making racket. Everyone comes here to make money.
The local sewage works is severely over-capacity. Raw sewage floods the Olifantsriver and its irrigation canals that dairy farmer Chris Keesh depends on.
CHRIS KEESH, CO-OWNER BAKENKRAAL DAIRY FARM: We can’t use the water at all – it leaves a dust on the ground and sticks to the lucern plant. It stays there for a long time until the stuff is cut and it’s poisonous for cattle, the cattle can die from it.
Local Afriforum chairman George Kersop has been keeping an eye on the mounting electricity bill. ESKOM has told us that they’ve taken legal steps to disconnect the town.
GEORGE KERSOP, AFRIFORUM: It’s R17-million in arrears still.
R33-million is due in early August.
Oudtshoorn was already cash-strapped and under investigation by the Special Investigations Unit when in 2010, 11 ANC councillors took power in coalition with one councillor from the National People’s Party and one from the Independent Civic Organisation of South Africa.
Two years in, five ANC councillors crossed the floor to the DA. A few months later, the DA won a by-election and solidified their majority – as they did a second time this year.
In the normal course of council business motions of no confidence would have followed with regard to the ANC Mayor, NPP Speaker and ICOSA deputy and the DA would fill those posts. Instead two years of court applications and counter applications followed as the NPP Speaker would not to let the motions be tabled – even up to June this year. Winning by-elections meant nothing. The DA couldn’t take over.
JOHN: So why should people in other parts of the country care about the local politics in Oudtshoorn? Well, who would have thought it possible that an entire municipality could have been brought to its knees, to the point where it can’t even pass a budget. The lesson is that if it can happen in Oudtshoorn, it can happen anywhere.
Editor Liesel le Roux reported on how judge after judge found against the minority coalition, cautioning against spending taxpayers’ money on court battles; and instructing the council to convene.
LIESEL LE ROUX: We had a bomb scare in the council, then we had the Speaker having a heart attack and every time we had a council meeting something happened so that there’s no council meeting and three months later something else happens, so there are many tricks you can use to stay in power, so I think this is a warning for the rest of SA.
Initially, local government lawyer Hardy Mills worked for the municipality, defending the Speaker’s suppressing motions of no confidence. But soon, Mills couldn’t square his work with his conscience – because he knew where his instructions were actually coming from.
HARDY MILLS: I’d say the main power and main control is vested in the Municipal Manager – politically and administratively…now, if you look at your municipal legislation, the MM is not a political appointment, he’s not supposed to be a political appointment, he must focus on administration – now in Oudtshoorn it’s not like that.
Acting Municipal Manager Ronnie Lottering left the South African Police Service as commander for covert operations in 2008. He was a member of the National People’s Party and on his CV lists controversial founder of the NPP Badhi Chabaan as a reference.
Lottering suspended economic development manager Greg Baartman six months ago. Greg had been named in 2011 SIU report on alledged double invoicing.
GREG BAARTMAN: Up to this hour there have been no charges served on me. The Bargaining Council agreement says that you have to bring charges against a person within three months, otherwise that person must come back.
As an ANC member Baartman believes Lottering needed a scapegoat when pressure from national government started mounting.
GREG BAARTMAN: The norm in the municipality these days is what they call in the supply chain process, deviations. There has to be an urgency and an emergency to be able to do the work. In most cases, in the era of Ronnie Lottering there’s neither urgency, nor emergency.
In February this year, armed with his team’s dire assessment of the municipality, Minister Pravin Gordhan paid a surprise visit to the town…
PRAVIN GORDHAN: We parked our vehicles at a shopping centre – walked through – asking them how they see their municipality – within 5 minutes we heard the complaints of the governance issues…we then went to the municipal offices – not a very nice response.
Lottering denied our request for an interview – but as fate would have it in a small town – we bumped into him out for lunch with a DA Councilor who would become mayor later that week.
RONNIE LOTTERING: This is not professional from you…this is a private lunch…I said come to my office eight o’ clock!
The next day Lottering honoured his appointment. He insisted he’d resigned from the NPP when he got this office and though the law says he may act in the position for only 90 days, he said shared the role at times with other officials as council had failed to appoint a permanent manager. And the caves? Well – it’s simple: The money belongs to the operational budget of this municipality, he said.
On the other allegations: DID YOU SUSPENDED GREG BAARTMAN FOR SIX MONTHS WITHOUT CHARGE?
RONNIE LOTTERING: He’s been charged. There’s a charge sheet for him, but I’m asking you not to mention his name, please.
Neither Baartman, nor his union IMATU, has received a charge sheet.
ARE DEVIATIONS THE NORM IN APPOINTING SERVICE PROVIDERS?
RONNIE LOTTERING: Ja, we will deviate, but it must be well-motivated. The deviations register is open for everyone, because we table that report in front of council. We will make it available.
When pressed for the register he’d offered, we were told to lodge a Promotion of Access to Information application.
DID YOU HAVE GANGSTERS TRANSPORTED IN YOUR CAR TO DISRUPT MEETINGS?
RONNIE LOTTERING: I’m the only driver of my vehicle – if there’s any of those allegations…I’m open for any investigation.
ARE YOU ONE OF THE MEN WHO BROKE DEMOCRACY IN THIS TOWN?
RONNIE LOTTERING: Democracy is a very good thing but you cannot set aside certain legislation just for the sake of democracy. The fact that the ANC, NPP, ICOSA coalition is still in charge of council is based to the operation of law, they must wait until the outcome of the appeal court case.
The so-manieth court judgement is expected in September. Until then a number of DA Councilors are precluded from voting. Minister Gordhan says the Constitution mandates him to spearhead an intergovernmental process to put Oudtshoorn under administration.
PRAVIN GORDAN: So I’m glad that for a few weeks now we are at one on the need for an intervention – putting in place an administrator and a team both from the province and national – we’re just waiting – within the next few days – information that will indicate that we’re making progress in this regard.
Meanwhile, Oudtshoorn residents were baffled to see NPP Speaker John Stoffels resign…only to resurface as deputy mayor in a new deal with the DA. Behind the scenes this horse-trading was referred to as the Jaegermeister Treaty.
JOHN: Why the Jaegermeister Treaty?
HARDY MILLS: Because you do stupid things when you drink too much Jaegermeister. Everyone was very surprised…although the DA have branded these two smaller parties as the devil…the tail is wagging the dog…the DA is the biggest party, ANC is second best, but there’s no doubt that the municipality is being controlled and run by the two small parties, ICOSA and NPP, so really, is that democracy?

PRAVIN GORDHAN: If we’re not looking after treasures like that in a municipal area…how can we say we’re governing a town in a decent and correct kind of way? OUDTSHOORN SCRIPT JOHN: Oudtshoorn is one of the Jewels on the Garden Route, Gateway to the Klein Karoo. But peel back the peaceful veneer, and what’s revealed, is a town held hostage by apparent vested interests and political expedience. MR X: What happened here is that on the Tuesday night… of this council meeting…is that people were transported to this specific council meeting… with Ronnie Lottering’s Fortuner. Mr X is a longtime resident of Oudtshoorn. Together with some councillors who wouldn’t go on camera, he said Municipal Manager Ronnie Lottering is the man who broke democracy in this town. Mr X: What happened here is that THOMAS tried to fight inside the council meeting to approve the budget. THOMAS is an element of the Americans. JOHN: So these are gangsters were talking about? MR X: Yes, he is a gangster. JOHN: You mention that you know what’s happening here because this is a role that you filled in the past. MR X: I was used repeatedly, phoned to come and transport the people. I collected people from the refuse dump...around 60 or 70 men that I transported. I was given R1000 now and then to give the men, then I used about R150 for fuel and the other R800 I gave the men. Municipalities all around South Africa face a crisis of capacity and corruption. When he assumed the Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs ministry last year, Pravin Gordhan undertook a thorough assessment of the job ahead. MINISTER PRAVIN GORDHAN, COOPERATIVE GOVERNANCE & TRADITIONAL AFFAIRS: we undertook an extensive desktop and sometimes physical study of municipalities – all 278 of them – categorised them into those that are doing well, those that are reasonably well but need to repair one or two things and those that are doing poorly – display some levels of dysfunctionality. Oudtshoorn stuck out as a sore thumb… The semi-arid Oudtshoorn, with its nearly 100-thousand residents rely on tourism and agriculture for survival – mismanaging resources could bring suffering that would be hard to recover from. Newspaper publisher Schalk le Roux has seen the rift between Oudtshoorn local municipality and its people widen. SCHALK LE ROUX, DIE HOORN PUBLISHER: At one point I even called it a hoodlum regime. They do exactly as they please. Processes aren’t followed – like with the appointment of people. When goods are purchased they don’t follow tender processes. They are just not accountable. The governance meltdown threatens one of our greatest national treasures. Archaeologist Hein Gerstner pours his heart and soul into stewarding the Cango Caves. JOHN: Hein, talk about the paper trail. What are we dealing with here? HEIN GERSTNER: Each and every one of these documents is an outcry over a number of years to say, what is happening under the municipal auspices, is not conducive to the caves and this is basically a plea to change that… The Caves have always been managed as a part of Oudtshoorn municipality. After 1994 surplus funds from admission fees and a loan taken out to build the museum complex was saved in an investment account – reserves for future cave maintenance and development. HEIN GERSTNER: In 2011 you noticed there’s an R17-million, R17,7-million in that particular fund. JOHN: These totals are substantially down from previous years, but I guess is it any wonder if you for example a figure of R5-million flowing out of the account? HEIN GERSTNER: At certain points this was reduced to a R139, which is…it’s very alarming to run a business if you have no control over your cash flow. A year ago Hein first blew the whistle on the dwindling millions, begging anyone who would listen to take the caves and the funds they generate from the municipality’s control. JOHN: What’s your best guess what this money is used for, why is it going to the municipality in the first place. HEIN GERSTNER: Well I can’t even speculate. I think it’s only for running the Municipality in general, because the situation is so desperate and dire. JOHN: So the caves are somewhat of a cash cow, “its money that’s there, let’s use the money”. President of Oudtshoorn’s tourism authority Niel Els says in the current economic climate, bad publicity threatens the whole region. NIEL ELS: The economic impact of the Cango caves on a small town like Oudtshoorn is annually round about 400 million and that’s only if you take the average visitor to the Cango Caves will only stay one night on Oudtshoorn. So we are really adamant that the Municipality should sort out their problems, so we can go ahead and market this town as best as possible. HEIN GERSTNER: I’m in my 23rd year of running the caves and I can’t constantly be fighting this battle just to keep the coffers open and the business open. JOHN: What are the consequences for you of talking to us? HEIN GERSTNER: It will be interesting to see but I feel it’s my responsibility as the custodian of that heritage and…you…(chokes up, gets up and walks away) At the end of his tether – Gerstner faces declining visitor numbers…a drained bank account…and desperate creditors, owed over R4-million for new light installations. The caves budget should be signed off by the local council by no later than the thirtieth of June every year. But for the last two years this and other council business has all but ground to a halt. JOHN: In-fighting in the Oudsthoorn Municipality has brought service delivery to a standstill. Roads, sewage, electricity, all have been impacted by the rot. MOTORIST VOXIE: Everything is done cheaply and in the long run the motorist suffers – check the potholes in the road. PEDESTRIAN VOXIE: It’s been re-done 10 times. It’s money-making racket. Everyone comes here to make money. The local sewage works is severely over-capacity. Raw sewage floods the Olifantsriver and its irrigation canals that dairy farmer Chris Keesh depends on. CHRIS KEESH, CO-OWNER BAKENKRAAL DAIRY FARM: We can’t use the water at all – it leaves a dust on the ground and sticks to the lucern plant. It stays there for a long time until the stuff is cut and it’s poisonous for cattle, the cattle can die from it. Local Afriforum chairman George Kersop has been keeping an eye on the mounting electricity bill. ESKOM has told us that they’ve taken legal steps to disconnect the town. GEORGE KERSOP, AFRIFORUM: It’s R17-million in arrears still. R33-million is due in early August. Oudtshoorn was already cash-strapped and under investigation by the Special Investigations Unit when in 2010, 11 ANC councillors took power in coalition with one councillor from the National People’s Party and one from the Independent Civic Organisation of South Africa. Two years in, five ANC councillors crossed the floor to the DA. A few months later, the DA won a by-election and solidified their majority – as they did a second time this year. In the normal course of council business motions of no confidence would have followed with regard to the ANC Mayor, NPP Speaker and ICOSA deputy and the DA would fill those posts. Instead two years of court applications and counter applications followed as the NPP Speaker would not to let the motions be tabled – even up to June this year. Winning by-elections meant nothing. The DA couldn’t take over. JOHN: So why should people in other parts of the country care about the local politics in Oudtshoorn? Well, who would have thought it possible that an entire municipality could have been brought to its knees, to the point where it can’t even pass a budget. The lesson is that if it can happen in Oudtshoorn, it can happen anywhere. Editor Liesel le Roux reported on how judge after judge found against the minority coalition, cautioning against spending taxpayers’ money on court battles; and instructing the council to convene. LIESEL LE ROUX: We had a bomb scare in the council, then we had the Speaker having a heart attack and every time we had a council meeting something happened so that there’s no council meeting and three months later something else happens, so there are many tricks you can use to stay in power, so I think this is a warning for the rest of SA. Initially, local government lawyer Hardy Mills worked for the municipality, defending the Speaker’s suppressing motions of no confidence. But soon, Mills couldn’t square his work with his conscience – because he knew where his instructions were actually coming from. HARDY MILLS: I’d say the main power and main control is vested in the Municipal Manager – politically and administratively…now, if you look at your municipal legislation, the MM is not a political appointment, he’s not supposed to be a political appointment, he must focus on administration – now in Oudtshoorn it’s not like that. Acting Municipal Manager Ronnie Lottering left the South African Police Service as commander for covert operations in 2008. He was a member of the National People’s Party and on his CV lists controversial founder of the NPP Badhi Chabaan as a reference. Lottering suspended economic development manager Greg Baartman six months ago. Greg had been named in 2011 SIU report on alledged double invoicing. GREG BAARTMAN: Up to this hour there have been no charges served on me. The Bargaining Council agreement says that you have to bring charges against a person within three months, otherwise that person must come back. As an ANC member Baartman believes Lottering needed a scapegoat when pressure from national government started mounting. GREG BAARTMAN: The norm in the municipality these days is what they call in the supply chain process, deviations. There has to be an urgency and an emergency to be able to do the work. In most cases, in the era of Ronnie Lottering there’s neither urgency, nor emergency. In February this year, armed with his team’s dire assessment of the municipality, Minister Pravin Gordhan paid a surprise visit to the town… PRAVIN GORDHAN: We parked our vehicles at a shopping centre – walked through – asking them how they see their municipality – within 5 minutes we heard the complaints of the governance issues…we then went to the municipal offices – not a very nice response. Lottering denied our request for an interview – but as fate would have it in a small town – we bumped into him out for lunch with a DA Councilor who would become mayor later that week. RONNIE LOTTERING: This is not professional from you…this is a private lunch…I said come to my office eight o’ clock! The next day Lottering honoured his appointment. He insisted he’d resigned from the NPP when he got this office and though the law says he may act in the position for only 90 days, he said shared the role at times with other officials as council had failed to appoint a permanent manager. And the caves? Well – it’s simple: The money belongs to the operational budget of this municipality, he said. On the other allegations: DID YOU SUSPENDED GREG BAARTMAN FOR SIX MONTHS WITHOUT CHARGE? RONNIE LOTTERING: He’s been charged. There’s a charge sheet for him, but I’m asking you not to mention his name, please. Neither Baartman, nor his union IMATU, has received a charge sheet. ARE DEVIATIONS THE NORM IN APPOINTING SERVICE PROVIDERS? RONNIE LOTTERING: Ja, we will deviate, but it must be well-motivated. The deviations register is open for everyone, because we table that report in front of council. We will make it available. When pressed for the register he’d offered, we were told to lodge a Promotion of Access to Information application. DID YOU HAVE GANGSTERS TRANSPORTED IN YOUR CAR TO DISRUPT MEETINGS? RONNIE LOTTERING: I’m the only driver of my vehicle – if there’s any of those allegations…I’m open for any investigation. ARE YOU ONE OF THE MEN WHO BROKE DEMOCRACY IN THIS TOWN? RONNIE LOTTERING: Democracy is a very good thing but you cannot set aside certain legislation just for the sake of democracy. The fact that the ANC, NPP, ICOSA coalition is still in charge of council is based to the operation of law, they must wait until the outcome of the appeal court case. The so-manieth court judgement is expected in September. Until then a number of DA Councilors are precluded from voting. Minister Gordhan says the Constitution mandates him to spearhead an intergovernmental process to put Oudtshoorn under administration. PRAVIN GORDAN: So I’m glad that for a few weeks now we are at one on the need for an intervention – putting in place an administrator and a team both from the province and national – we’re just waiting – within the next few days – information that will indicate that we’re making progress in this regard. Meanwhile, Oudtshoorn residents were baffled to see NPP Speaker John Stoffels resign…only to resurface as deputy mayor in a new deal with the DA. Behind the scenes this horse-trading was referred to as the Jaegermeister Treaty. JOHN: Why the Jaegermeister Treaty? HARDY MILLS: Because you do stupid things when you drink too much Jaegermeister. Everyone was very surprised…although the DA have branded these two smaller parties as the devil…the tail is wagging the dog…the DA is the biggest party, ANC is second best, but there’s no doubt that the municipality is being controlled and run by the two small parties, ICOSA and NPP, so really, is that democracy?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Two years after losing their seats on the Oudtshoorn town council, members of the now minority ANC/NPP coalition flatly refuse to vacate their posts - the town hovers on the brink of bankruptcy
metadata.Summary: Oudtshoorn is on a knife edge with politicians on all sides pleading for national governement and senior ANC intervention. We expect motion of no-confidence this coming week in municipal manager Ronnie Lottering. Speaker John Sotffels surprisingly resigned last week. We investigate allegations that Mayor Gordon April, Ronnie Lottering and publicity consultant Drewan Baird have been manipulating the system, holding on to power for personal gain - running the council like their personal fiefdom. The council stopped working two years ago after the ANC-coalition refused to hand over power to the DA-COPE coalition. Municipal budgets are not being passed - resulting in the non-payment of services - for instance, in less than a month, the town is due to be disconnected form the electicity grid by ESKOM to whom it owes around R25-million. The local river, a water source for the region, is being polluted by raw sewage, as service provision grinds to a halt. Money has been misallocated from the budget of the Cango Caves - an important regional, if not national, tourist attraction and significant income earner. The council has refused to hold meetings; suspended councillors for no reason; allegedly used public money in litigation as a delaying tactic; have allegedly offered inducements to other councillors in exchange for votes; and have ignored court orders. Protests flared in March when municipal workers heard the municipality had allegedly stolen their pension and medical aid contributions. It reached fever pitch this week when fisticuffs broke out in the council chamber after town councillors failed to approve the municipality’s budget for the third time in two months. The public gallery got involved in barricading councillors for two hours after the DA voted against the budget and the ANC abstained. Both the ANC and the DA-led provincial government put out statements pleading with Cooperative Governance Minister Pravin Gordhan to intervene.
metadata.Further information: The town council became paralysed by infighting after May 2013, when the DA seized control of the ANC-run municipality -- five ANC councillors voted with the DA in a motion of no confidence in the speaker, mayor and deputy mayor. In September 2013 the Western Cape High Court ruled that the DA’s ‘takeover’ of the Oudtshoorn municipality in this manner was illegitimate. By then, however, by-elections had handed the DA a clear council majority in a coalition with Cope. Subsequent by-elections have also seen the ANC lose. In May this year, the DA won another ward. The DA has a council majority on paper, but the ANC in coalition with some smaller parties steadfastly refuses to relinquish power. In May, DA Western Cape leader Patricia de Lille wrote to President Jacob Zuma to intervene. The ANC Western Cape leader Marius Fransman has suggested that the council may need to be dissolved. Gordhan did visit the municipality in March and proposed a "support and good governance package", which the municipality subsequently failed to adopt. Such a package would include the appointment of an experienced municipal manager, and would also seek to resolve outstanding legal matters affecting municipal operations. In June, a letter signed by all the DA councillors in the municipality and seven out of the 10 ANC councillors called for the adoption of Gordhan's package and they stated that their concern for the state of the municipality transcended their party affiliations. Gordhan has said that he would be visiting Outdshoorn again to discuss the implementation of government support. ANC Western Cape local government spokesperson Richard Dyanti called on councillors to work with Gordhan “to ensure the rescue package put together for the Little Karoo town is put in motion to work optimally for the people”. Western Cape MEC Bredell, meanwhile, noted “with concern” the “continued instability” in the Oudtshoorn council, and said that he remained in “continuous consultation” with Minister Gordhan.
